hints: Think about why a tiny peak appears at one mass unit above the molecular ion, and which element present in $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ is responsible for it.
walkthrough:
Spot what the two peaks are**
You have $m/e = 74$ which is the molecular ion $M^+$ of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ ($4 \times 12 + 10 \times 1 + 16 = 74$). The tiny peak at $m/e = 75$ is the $M+1$ peak, caused by molecules containing one heavier isotope, essentially one $^{13}\text{C}$ instead of $^{12}\text{C}$.

Use the 1.1% rule for carbon**
Each carbon atom contributes about 1.1% of the intensity of the $M$ peak to the $M+1$ peak. With 4 carbons: $$\text{expected M+1} = 4 \times 1.1\% \times \text{abundance of M} = 0.044 \times 50 = 2.2$$ So $x = 2.2$.

hints: For each $m/e$ value, try combinations of C (12), H (1) and O (16) from $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ that add up to that mass, remembering the fragment must carry a + charge.
Check that $m/e = 29$ can be made without oxygen, while $m/e = 59$ needs a combination that includes oxygen to reach the correct mass.
walkthrough:
Treat fragments as jigsaw pieces of W**
W is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. In the mass spectrometer the molecular ion breaks apart, and each positively charged piece is detected at its mass to charge ratio. Since charge is +1, $m/e$ is simply the mass of the fragment ion.

Solve m/e = 29**
Try carbons and hydrogens only: $2 \times 12 + 5 \times 1 = 24 + 5 = 29$. That fits perfectly, so the ion is $$[\text{C}_2\text{H}_5]^+$$ This is a very common ethyl fragment.

Solve m/e = 59**
Try including the oxygen: $3 \times 12 + 7 \times 1 + 16 = 36 + 7 + 16 = 59$. That fits, so the ion is $$[\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{O}]^+$$ This tells you W contains a three carbon fragment still attached to oxygen.

hints: Read the wavenumber of the centre of absorption A in Fig. 5.1 and absorption B in Fig. 5.2, then match each to the ranges in Table 5.2.
walkthrough: Absorption A is the broad O–H absorption near $3300\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, identifying a hydroxy (alcohol) group.

Absorption B is the strong C=O absorption near $1710\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. X has no broad O–H absorption, including the broad $2500$–$3000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ band expected for a carboxylic acid. Identify the group as carbonyl (ketone).
Table 5.3: A — O–H, hydroxy/alcohol; B — C=O, carbonyl/ketone.

hints: Use both the carbonyl absorption and the absence of a broad O–H absorption in X. Consider the final products when primary and secondary alcohols are heated under reflux with excess oxidant.
walkthrough: W is an alcohol, but X contains C=O and has no broad O–H absorption. X is therefore not a carboxylic acid. An aldehyde would be further oxidised under reflux with excess acidified dichromate, so X is a ketone.
The only secondary alcohol with formula $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}$ is butan-2-ol. Oxidising its CH(OH) group gives butan-2-one: $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CH_3+[O]\rightarrow CH_3C(=O)CH_2CH_3+H_2O}$.
Draw X as $\mathrm{CH_3C(=O)CH_2CH_3}$. The mass fragments in (a) are consistent with the four-carbon alcohol; the oxidation conditions and IR spectrum distinguish the ketone from an acid.

hints: Y gives hydrogen with sodium so it has $\text{O}-\text{H}$, but it is not oxidised by acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$. Ask yourself which class of alcohol resists oxidation.
walkthrough:
Narrow down Y from the tests**
Bubbles with sodium means Y has an acidic hydrogen, here an alcohol $\text{O}-\text{H}$. But Y does not react with acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$. Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised, tertiary alcohols have no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the $\text{OH}$ and cannot be oxidised. So Y must contain a tertiary alcohol group.
Final answer: tertiary alcohol (tertiary hydroxy group)

hints: Recall the general reaction of an alcohol with sodium to form a sodium alkoxide plus hydrogen, then apply it to $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Write the pattern then fill in**
Think of alcohol as $\text{ROH}$. With sodium: $$2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_2$$ Here $\text{R} = \text{C}_4\text{H}_9$. Substituting gives $$2\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2$$ The colourless bubbles observed are the $\text{H}_2$ gas.

hints: Y is a $\text{C}_4$ tertiary alcohol that does not give a yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_2$(aq), so draw the only tertiary $\text{C}_4$ alcohol structure.
walkthrough:
Use all clues to pin down the skeleton**
Y is an isomer of W, so $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$, and a tertiary alcohol. There is only one tertiary butanol: a central carbon joined to three $\text{CH}_3$ groups and one $\text{OH}$, i.e. $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$.

Check the negative iodoform test**
Warming with alkaline $\text{I}_2$(aq) gives a yellow precipitate only with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ groups. 2-methylpropan-2-ol has no such group, so no reaction, exactly as observed. This confirms Y is 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
